n: Jephthah is a brave warrior but an outsider — the son of a prostitute. God often works through people others reject.

f.g: Gilead is both his father’s name and the name of the region.

n: His half-brothers drive him out so he can’t share the inheritance.

f.g: A woman outside the family — here, a prostitute.

n: Jephthah flees to Tob, northeast of Gilead, where a band of rough, landless men gathers around him — much like David’s band later.

f.g: Empty-handed, restless men; adventurers.
A region east of the Jordan, probably in southern Syria.

n: In time, the Ammonites go to war against Israel.

f.g: After some time.

n: Gilead’s elders swallow their pride and go to bring Jephthah back.
They ask him to be their military commander.

f.g: Hebrew qatsin, a military commander.

n: Jephthah points out the irony: you hated me and threw me out — and now you come to me in trouble?
The elders up their offer: lead us in battle and be head over all Gilead.

f.g: Hebrew rosh, ruler — a higher position than “captain.”

n: Jephthah negotiates carefully: if the Lord gives me victory, will I truly be your head?

f.w: the LORD deliver them before me
f.g: Jephthah credits success to the Lord from the start.

n: The elders swear an oath with the Lord as witness.

f.w: The LORD be witness between us

n: Jephthah is made head and commander, and he repeats the agreement before the Lord at Mizpeh, making it a sacred covenant.

f.w: uttered all his words before the LORD
f.g: Formally confirmed the agreement in God’s presence.

n: Before fighting, Jephthah tries diplomacy, asking the Ammonite king why he has invaded.

f.w: What hast thou to do with me
f.g: “What quarrel do you have with me?”

n: Ammon claims Israel stole its land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers when coming from Egypt, and demands it back.

f.g: Two rivers flowing west into the Dead Sea and Jordan, marking the region east of the Jordan.

n: Jephthah sends a second, longer message — a careful historical argument.

f.g: Persistence in seeking peace before war.

n: First point: Israel never took land from Moab or Ammon.
He recounts Israel’s journey from Egypt through the wilderness to Kadesh.
Israel politely asked Edom and Moab for passage and was refused, so it stayed at Kadesh rather than force its way.

f.w: king of Edom would not hearken

n: Israel went around Edom and Moab, never entering Moab’s territory, which ended at the Arnon.

f.g: Went around.

f.w: Arnon was the border of Moab

n: Israel asked Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, for passage too.
Sihon refused, gathered his army at Jahaz, and attacked Israel.
God gave Israel victory, and Israel took the Amorites’ land — not Ammon’s.
That is how Israel came to own the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

f.g: Territory.

n: Since Israel’s God gave the land, what right does Ammon have to it?

f.g: Drove out.

n: Jephthah speaks in terms the king would understand: you keep what your god Chemosh gives you; we keep what the Lord gives us.

f.g: Chiefly the god of Moab; Jephthah may treat Ammon and Moab as one claim.

n: Not even Balak of Moab, who hired Balaam, ever went to war over this land.
Israel had held these towns for three hundred years. Why wait until now to claim them? This rough figure helps scholars estimate the period of the judges.

f.g: A round figure for the time since the conquest.
A town on the Arnon gorge.

n: Jephthah rests his case: we have not wronged you. Let the Lord, the true Judge, decide between us.
The Ammonite king ignores his reasoning.

f.g: Would not listen.

n: The Spirit of the Lord comes upon Jephthah, and he gathers troops through Gilead and Manasseh to attack.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah

n: Then Jephthah makes a vow, offering God something in return for victory — though the Spirit had already come upon him. He didn’t need to bargain.

f.g: Surely.

n: He vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him will be the Lord’s, offered as a burnt offering. The Hebrew can mean “whoever,” a reckless promise in a home where people would come out.

f.g: Hebrew can read “whoever comes out.”
An offering wholly given to God.

n: Jephthah fights Ammon, and the Lord gives him victory.

f.g: The victory is credited to God.

n: He wins a great victory across twenty Ammonite towns, and Ammon is subdued.

f.g: Hebrew Abel-keramim, a place name.

n: Coming home, his only child — his daughter — rushes out dancing to celebrate, as women did after victories. The joy turns instantly to grief.

f.g: Hand drums or tambourines.

n: Jephthah tears his clothes in grief. He feels he cannot take back his vow to the Lord.

f.g: Tore his clothing, a sign of deep mourning.

n: His daughter shows remarkable faith and courage: keep your vow, since the Lord has given you victory.

f.w: do to me according to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth
f.g: She accepts the vow’s consequences for her father’s sake.

n: She asks for two months to go into the hills with her friends to mourn that she will never marry or have children.

f.g: Mourn that she would die, or live, without marriage or children.

n: He lets her go, and she mourns with her companions in the mountains.

f.g: Friends.

n: She returns and her father fulfills his vow. Interpreters differ: many think he sacrificed her, which God’s law condemned; others note the stress that “she knew no man” and think she was dedicated to lifelong unmarried service at the sanctuary.

f.w: did with her according to his vow
f.g: The Lord forbade human sacrifice; the text neither approves nor explains the act.
She never married.

n: Every year Israel’s young women honored her for four days. The story stands as a tragic warning against rash vows and as a memorial to a faithful daughter.

f.g: Possibly “to commemorate” or “to recount.”
